title: What is inflation and why does it happen?
seoTitle: What Is Inflation? Causes, Effects and Central Bank Policy Explained
seoDescription: Learn what inflation is, how it is measured, what causes it, how it affects households and markets, and why central banks respond with interest rates.
excerpt: Inflation is a broad rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money over time.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: Inflation means a broad increase in the prices of goods and services, not just one expensive item.
It can be driven by demand, supply constraints, input costs, wages, expectations and monetary conditions.
Inflation reduces purchasing power when incomes do not rise as quickly as prices.
Central banks typically use interest rates to influence demand, but policy works with delays and trade-offs.
body: Inflation describes a general increase in prices across an economy over time. When inflation rises, one unit of currency buys fewer goods and services than before.

That does not mean every price rises at the same speed. Housing, energy, food and services can move very differently, which is why households may experience inflation differently from official averages.

sections.heading: How inflation is measured
paragraphs: Statistical agencies track baskets of goods and services and calculate how their prices change over time. Consumer price indexes are among the most common measures.

Different indexes use different baskets and methodologies. Headline inflation may include volatile food and energy prices, while core measures often exclude some volatile categories to reveal broader underlying trends.

sections.heading: Demand-driven inflation
paragraphs: If demand grows faster than an economy's ability to produce goods and services, businesses may raise prices. This can happen when households, companies or governments increase spending strongly while capacity is limited.
Demand pressure is especially important when labor markets are tight and spare production capacity is low.

sections.heading: Supply shocks and cost pressure
paragraphs: Inflation can also come from the supply side. Energy shortages, shipping disruptions, crop failures or shortages of key components can increase the cost of production.
Businesses may pass some of those costs to customers. If the shock is broad enough, overall inflation can rise even while economic growth slows.

sections.heading: Wages, expectations and persistence
paragraphs: Workers may demand higher wages when living costs rise. Higher wages can support household demand but also increase costs for businesses, especially in labor-intensive services.

Inflation expectations matter because they can influence wage negotiations, pricing decisions and contracts. If people expect high inflation to persist, those expectations can make inflation harder to reduce.

sections.heading: Why central banks raise rates
paragraphs: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive and can reduce demand for mortgages, investment and consumption. They also increase the return available on safer savings instruments.
The aim is to reduce excess demand and bring inflation back toward target. But monetary policy works with delays, and aggressive tightening can weaken growth and employment.

sections.heading: How inflation affects markets and households
paragraphs: Inflation can erode real wages and cash savings if income and interest do not keep pace. It can also influence bond yields, currency values and company profit margins.
For businesses, the impact depends on pricing power, input costs, debt structure and demand. There is no single asset that always benefits from inflation in every environment.

faq.question: Is all inflation bad?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Many central banks target a low positive inflation rate because moderate inflation can coexist with economic growth and helps avoid persistent deflation.

faq.question: What is deflation?
faq.answer: Deflation is a broad decline in prices over time. Persistent deflation can weaken spending and increase the real burden of debt.

faq.question: Why can inflation fall while prices stay high?
faq.answer: Lower inflation means prices are rising more slowly, not necessarily returning to previous levels.
